articles.title: Gold, silver price outlook: US-Iran tensions, inflation data to set the tone next week
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Gold and silver may have ended the week on a brighter note, but whether they can keep the shine going is another question.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Gold and silver may have ended the week on a brighter note, but whether they can keep the shine going is another question. Bullion prices could remain under pressure next week as investors brace for a busy mix of inflation data, crude oil movements and fresh twists in the US-Iran conflict.Both precious metals managed to finish the week with gains in domestic and international markets. However, the recovery may not be enough to signal a sustained turnaround. Investors will be keeping a close eye on inflation readings from major economies for clues on the interest rate outlook, while geopolitical tensions and peace negotiations could add to the uncertainty.With several factors pulling prices in different directions, will gold and silver find their footing or face another bout of volatility?Here are the key triggers to watch next week.Inflation data and Fed commentary in focusA series of inflation releases from China, the US, Germany, Japan and India will be closely watched by investors. The readings could provide clues about the direction of interest rates and influence sentiment towards precious metals.Speeches by Federal Reserve officials and US employment data will also remain on the market's radar. Investors will assess these developments alongside movements in crude oil prices to gauge the broader economic outlook."Gold and silver's momentum remains down as investors will focus on the inflation data from China, the US, Germany, Japan, India, etc along with some Fed officials' commentary," said Pranav Mer, senior vice president, EBG - Commodity & currency research, JM Financial Services Ltd.Chinese economic indicators will also be important, particularly for industrial metals, analysts said.Geopolitical developments are likely to remain another major factor for bullion prices. US President Donald Trump confirmed fresh military strikes on Iran but also said Washington had made "a lot of progress" in negotiations with Tehran.The developments have left investors tracking both the conflict and the possibility of a diplomatic resolution.Mer said markets would also watch progress in peace negotiations between the US and Iran to end the war, as well as the Russia-Ukraine peace talks.Gold and silver recover after a volatile weekThe domestic and international bullion markets recorded weekly gains, despite facing pressure earlier in the week.On the Multi Commodity Exchange, December gold futures rose Rs 3,682, or nearly 3%, over the past week to close at Rs 1.42 lakh per 10 grams. Silver futures gained Rs 5,655, or 3.15%, to settle at Rs 1.84 lakh per kilogram.Overseas, Comex gold futures for December delivery advanced $176, or 4.5%, to close at $4,074.9 per ounce. Silver futures climbed $2.6, or 5.4%, to settle at $51.94 per ounce.Explaining the price movement, Mer said stronger-than-expected US nonfarm payroll data and improving consumer sentiment initially weighed on bullion. These developments lifted the dollar and Treasury yields, putting pressure on gold and silver."However, prices ended with a strong weekly gain of more than 4 per cent in global markets, following a sharp rally mid-week after the US midterm election outcome that showed Democrats sweeping wins in both the Senate and the House over the Republicans," he added.Bargain buying supports recovery, but gains remain limitedPrecious metals found support during the week as investors bought at lower price levels and traders covered short positions. However, a correction in industrial metals, particularly copper, restricted the gains.The decline in AI, data centre and technology stocks across global markets, especially in the US, also supported bullion by encouraging demand for safe-haven assets.The recovery, however, faced another bout of selling towards the end of the week. According to Mer, gold and silver futures came under pressure on Friday, closing at around $4,074 and $52 per ounce, respectively.Domestic bullion prices could see moderate fluctuations next week as traders respond to international price movements, currency changes and inflation trends.Festive demand around Diwali will also be among the factors influencing domestic trading. The commodity market will remain closed during the morning session on Tuesday due to Diwali-Balipratipada.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Members of the Art for Guernsey team met with the group to hand over the donation.
articles.body:
Money raised by an art exhibition has been donated to help with the costs of 10 goats imported to introduce new bloodlines to Guernsey's goat population.

The Royal Golden Guernsey Goat Foundation was set up as part of the effort to protect and promote the breed on its native island.

More than £2,500 has been donated by Art for Guernsey from the sale of artworks that featured in the goat-themed exhibition that was held in their Mansell Street gallery in May.

Members of the Art for Guernsey team met with the foundation committee and its patron the Lieutenant-Governor Lt Gen Sir Richard Cripwell at Government House to announce the donation.

Sir Richard said: "Art for Guernsey's goat exhibition brought out the best in the island's artistic talent, engaged local school children and has directly benefited this special breed.

"It shows great initiative and the power of art for a good cause.

"I am grateful to David and his team for their initiative and support."

articles.title: Indian Oil plans to buy its own oil, LPG ships as freight costs surge 4 times
articles.summary: With shipping costs rising sharply and movement around the Strait of Hormuz facing disruptions, Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) is looking to take greater
articles.body: With shipping costs rising sharply and movement around the Strait of Hormuz facing disruptions, Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) is looking to take greater control of how its crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) reach its refineries.The state-owned oil major plans to purchase its own carriers and is also exploring the possibility of getting ships built in India.IOC's board has approved the purchase of a few vessels, and tenders for the proposed acquisitions were issued several months ago, director of finance Anuj Jain said during the company's second-quarter earnings call."The country needs oil sector companies to focus more on the shipping area now," Jain said, adding that the company was examining shipbuilding opportunities in India under the government's Make in India initiative.The proposed purchases could change the way IOC manages its shipping requirements. The company has traditionally depended on time-chartered and voyage-chartered vessels but is now looking at a combination of owning ships, improving existing charter arrangements and encouraging domestic shipbuilding.Shipping costs jump as Hormuz disruptions tighten the squeezeThe rising cost of transporting crude oil and LPG has made shipping arrangements an important part of IOC's strategy. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have disrupted commercial movement near the Strait of Hormuz, leading to higher freight rates and war-risk insurance costs.IOC currently has three crude oil carriers and nine LPG vessels under time-charter arrangements. These have helped it contain transportation expenses during the current crisis, Jain said.The difference between chartered and spot-market rates has been particularly sharp. IOC pays around $2-2.50 per barrel for its time-chartered crude carriers, against spot-market rates of up to $8-10 per barrel.The pressure is even more pronounced in LPG transportation. Freight rates that would generally be around $40 per tonne have climbed to $160-180 per tonne in the spot market, Jain said.Russia accounts for 55% of IOC's crude sourcingAlongside its plans to strengthen shipping capacity, IOC has changed the geographical mix of its crude purchases to diversify supplies and limit exposure to disruptions.Russia supplied 55 per cent of the company's crude requirements in the first half of the current financial year. Middle Eastern countries accounted for another 24 per cent, while Africa contributed around 10 per cent.Brazil supplied 7 per cent of IOC's crude, the United States accounted for 2-5 per cent and Venezuela contributed 3-4 per cent, Jain said.The company has also moved towards greater reliance on spot purchases. These accounted for around 87 per cent of its crude sourcing in the first half of FY27, against approximately 50 per cent in the previous financial year.IOC has managed to negotiate discounts against benchmark prices despite fluctuations in the global market. The premium or discount paid over benchmark crude during the September quarter ranged from a discount of $5 per barrel to a premium of $12 per barrel. In the preceding quarter, the range was between zero and a premium of $18 per barrel.Jain said IOC continued to purchase Russian crude at what it described as optimal prices and was also processing Venezuelan crude.Crude prices climb to around $120 per barrel in OctoberThe company's procurement strategy comes amid a sharp rise in oil prices following the escalation of US-Iran hostilities towards the end of February.Indian basket crude, which averaged around $65-70 per barrel in February, stayed above $100 for much of the first quarter. It averaged approximately $120 per barrel in October, Jain said.Despite the supply-chain challenges, IOC has kept its refinery operations at optimal levels while building up inventories to provide a buffer against disruptions.Its crude oil inventory has increased to around 39 days from the usual 33-35 days. The company was also holding 20 days of LPG inventory and 23-25 days of petrol and diesel stocks.Inventory gains help IOC report Rs 21,630 crore profitIOC's net profit rose to Rs 21,630 crore in the September quarter, compared with a loss of Rs 2,661 crore in the preceding quarter. The company had reported a profit of Rs 7,610 crore in the corresponding period last year.Inventory gains and improved performance across several businesses contributed to the quarterly profitability, the company said.IOC recorded a gross refining margin of $18.52 per barrel, excluding the impact of the special additional excise duty. Its inventory gain stood at Rs 6,948 crore during the quarter.However, the company continues to face uncertainty from geopolitical developments. Jain said these remained a key concern, particularly because of their impact on crude procurement, freight costs and marketing margins.IOC's plans to acquire vessels and explore shipbuilding in India come as it looks to strengthen its control over transportation alongside diversifying its crude purchases.You use AI every day. articles.summary: The US economy faces another important week of data releases, with inflation, housing sales and unemployment figures likely to offer fresh insights into
articles.body: The US economy faces another important week of data releases, with inflation, housing sales and unemployment figures likely to offer fresh insights into the financial pressures facing consumers and businesses.The focus comes as American households continue to deal with high prices of everyday essentials, from petrol to groceries. The latest updates follow the US midterm elections, in which Democrats swept Congress, a week ago.The economic situation has also been shaped by the war between the US and Iran, which began in February and cut global oil supplies. The resulting rise in energy costs added to inflationary pressures that were already high because of President Donald Trump's unpredictable tariff conflict with much of the world.Economists, investors and policymakers will be watching the upcoming numbers to assess how the war and tariffs continue to affect prices, the housing market and employment.US inflation: October CPI and PPI figures in focusThe first major update will come on Tuesday, when the US releases its consumer price index (CPI) data for October. Economists expect inflation to rise to 3.9%, against 3.7% in September.The CPI tracks price movements across a broad range of goods and services. Inflation has remained above 3% since March, following the start of the US war with Iran in February. The conflict led to a sharp rise in energy prices, which pushed up petrol prices and shipping costs.Businesses will also get a fresh reading of their costs on Friday, when the October producer price index (PPI) is released. Unlike the CPI, the PPI measures price changes before goods and services reach consumers.The September PPI report had recorded its biggest increase since December 2022. It also showed how higher fuel costs, particularly for diesel, were feeding into shipping and warehousing expenses.However, crude prices fell sharply over the past week after the US midterm elections. Some believe Democrats, who routed President Donald Trump's GOP, will push to end the Iran conflict, which has sent energy prices soaring.US housing market: Home sales expected to remain weakThe housing market will be another area of focus, with high property prices and rising interest rates continuing to weigh on homebuyers.The National Association of Realtors will release its October existing home sales report on Thursday. Economists expect the number of previously occupied homes sold to remain largely unchanged from September.The slowdown is not new. Home sales have remained close to an annual pace of 4 million since 2023, well below the historical average of around 5.2 million.Property prices have continued to rise despite the sluggish sales activity. Home prices have recorded annual increases for 39 consecutive months. At the same time, the average interest rate on a benchmark 30-year mortgage is hovering near its highest level in almost three years.Borrowing costs could remain high as the Federal Reserve considers another increase in its benchmark interest rate at its December meeting. The move would be aimed at cooling inflation, which has remained stubbornly high.US jobs market: Weekly claims to follow October's job gainsEmployment data will provide another measure of the economy's health. The US is scheduled to release its weekly unemployment claims figures on Thursday.Economists track these numbers because they offer an indication of layoffs and can help assess where the jobs market is headed. The latest weekly data showed that unemployment claims remained at historically low levels.The broader employment market has held up, with US employers adding 165,000 jobs in October. However, there are signs that workers are facing growing pressure.Wage increases have been slow and have not kept pace with inflation, leaving households struggling with the rising cost of living. While layoffs have largely remained in check, workers who lose their jobs are finding it increasingly difficult to secure new employment.Corporate earnings: CoreWeave, Cisco and SkyDance results dueBeyond economic indicators, investors will also track a series of corporate earnings announcements for clues about the artificial intelligence industry, data centres and Hollywood.CoreWeave is scheduled to announce its quarterly results on Tuesday, following a difficult week for AI-related stocks. The data centre company is seen by some as more exposed to rising borrowing costs. Its shares dropped close to 20% over the past week.Cisco and Applied Materials will report their results on Thursday.In the entertainment industry, SkyDance is set to post its earnings on Monday. articles.title: Unrest in France looks like a ‘pretty big foreshadowing’ to economists nervously eyeing national debt at 126% of GDP
articles.summary: "To me, the biggest warning sign from France is really not just the K-shaped economy effect, but the generational effect that's going on and to see young peo...
articles.body:
When U.S. markets watched as Paris metaphorically imploded just weeks ago, the consensus reaction was: "Let's not do that."

Unrest ripped through the French capital after protesters initially highlighted failings in the public school system. The action snowballed into widespread expressions of dissatisfaction with the cost of living and job prospects.

The macroeconomic health of the European nation is not in great shape: unemployment was 8.3% in Q2, real GDP growth was 0.4%, and wage growth was 1.7% at the national level. And underpinning it all is public debt, currently at 116% of GDP, with 30-year bonds topping 5.4% at the time of writing.

And the U.S. bond market, flirting with a wrap on the wrist for its own policymakers presiding over mounting debt , stalled. In fact, 10- and 30-year Treasury yields even declined.

"There's a reason that the U.S. has pulled back a little bit in the last few weeks [and] why France has not," Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told a Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC) event last week. "It's a couple of key indicators that differentiate us from France and suggest … that we still have a little bit of room to have these debates now, in the context of a K-shaped economy.

"We're at about 100% debt-to-GDP; they're at 120% debt-to-GDP. They are further along that crisis curve, and they are growing at about 0.5%. We're growing at just over 2%. That's a pretty big difference. "

While economists largely agree that policymakers are perhaps naive in their hopes to simply grow the U.S. out of a debt crisis, starting from a point of strength rather than stagnation gives the economy a better chance of rebalancing its debt-to-GDP ratio.

But Long added that France also differs from the U.S. in that the former has exhausted much of its revenue-generating capacity through taxes. Per the OECD, the "tax wedge" (the difference between labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee) for French workers is 47.2%, according to its most recent data. The U.S., on the other hand, is down at 30%.

"It's certainly not easy to raise taxation in the U.S., but from a financial world perspective and the bond market perspective, there's a lot more room to experiment and to grow in the United States than there is in France," Long added. "To me, the biggest warning sign from France is really not just the K-shaped economy effect, but the generational effect that's going on and to see young people really driving this latest protest … from the disparities that they're seeing generationally, and that seems like a pretty big foreshadowing [of] what we could see here as we creep towards 120% debt to GDP."

articles.title: Democrats won Congress. Can they actually stop Trump’s tariffs?
articles.summary: On the heels of their resounding victories in the midterms, Democrats are preparing to take President Trump’s tariffs head-on as part of their pledge to lower the cost of living. The tariffs, a central part of Trump’s economic agenda dating to his first term, were a frequent target for Democratic lawmakers and candidates on the…
articles.body:
On the heels of their resounding victories in the midterms , Democrats are preparing to take President Trump’s tariffs head-on as part of their pledge to lower the cost of living.

The tariffs , a central part of Trump’s economic agenda dating to his first term, were a frequent target for Democratic lawmakers and candidates on the trail.

After Democrats clinched majorities in both chambers of Congress, party leaders have already vowed to try and stop them through legislation.

“We need to stop the Trump tariffs that have increased costs on everyday Americans by thousands of dollars,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) told reporters on Wednesday.

How Democrats can do this once they assume the majority in both chambers could take different forms, Erica York, a senior economist at the Tax Foundation, told The Hill.

“It could be really narrow and just say, ‘These particular tariffs that the president has imposed, we want to … overrule those or … remove those from the books,’” she said of potential legislation.

She added, “It could be more expansive and say, ‘This authority in general shouldn’t sit with the president, and so we want to bring that back to Congress and not let any president do any tariff under this type of authority.’”

Arun Venkataraman, an international trade lawyer with Covington & Burling LLP who previously served in senior roles at the Commerce Department, said he sees Democrats getting more support “for specific tariff actions than they are to do a broadside against underlying” authorities.

“I don’t think we’re going to see them out of the gate on day one completely try to revise all of the U.S. trade laws,” he said. “I think that perhaps the more focused and strategic approach is to address particular tariffs, and then be able to get Republican support for some of that.”

Trump, however, still holds the veto power , a fact that he has repeated since Tuesday’s blue wave .

“I have the ultimate power — it’s called ‘veto.’” Trump told CBS News earlier this week.

The president even posted a photo of a red, MAGA-style hat with “VETO” written in big, white letters on Truth Social. The hat was also on the resolute desk on Thursday.

Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority, but it would require support from Democrats and Republicans. Multiple GOP critics of the tariffs, including Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), are also on their way out.

“They’re going to have to build a coalition that breaks that two-third veto, and that’s my concern,” said Kyle Sweetser, who owns a construction company in Alabama and has vocally opposed Trump’s tariffs.

“I think right now, if we zero in on tariffs … we can get a two-thirds vote on a solution here,” added Sweetser, who ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic Senate nomination in Alabama this cycle.

But Pierre Yared, who previously served on the White House Council of Economic Advisers during the second Trump administration, wrote that change in congressional control is unlikely to be enough on its own to change tariff policy.

“I expect the tariff policy to continue to remain largely under the president’s control, though the future direction of tariffs is subject to legal challenges as well as negotiations with trading partners,” wrote Yared , now a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Venkataraman said that “there have been a lot of people that have maybe been a little bit quick to dismiss the notion of a veto-proof majority.”

“Given the numbers that we saw with the elections this week, it is not completely implausible, and, to my mind, it is well worth the effort because there are Republican members that share these concerns and who heard directly from constituents,” he said.

Trump has imposed tariffs under multiple sections of federal law, including Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

The Supreme Court in February struck down the levies the president imposed last year under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

Section 232 and Section 338 allow the president to tax imports under national security concerns or after determining certain countries have discriminatory trade practices, respectively. Trump has cited the former statute in taxing steel, copper and aluminum imports, and slapped 50 percent levies on a slew of Canadian goods under the latter.

But the Constitution gives taxation power to Congress, and many Democrats now want to claw that back with their new majorities .

“Congress reclaiming its authority over tariffs and taking away those tariff rates,” is a major priority, Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) told The Bulwark before the election.

Boyle, who cruised to reelection and is in line to chair the House Budget Committee, added that Congress overturning Trump’s tariffs would equate to a “de facto tax cut” for Americans.

The data backs that up. As of August, Trump’s tariffs had added an average of $820 to U.S. households’ costs, according to the Tax Foundation .

York noted that is lower than what the organization estimated for 2025, as Trump’s IEEPA tariffs took effect in April of that year.

Obstacles remain in the way of Democrats’ eventual push to reel in the tariffs, however. York cited differing views between the free trade and protectionist wings of the party, arguing it could result in “tension” between lawmakers come January.

But even if Democrats coalesce and pass legislation, Trump will likely not accept limitations on his authority, rendering such a bill dead on arrival without a veto-proof majority.

“This is a big thing for him. He’s been supportive of tariffs for 30, 40 years,” Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican strategist, told The Hill this week.

Administration officials are also doubling down on the levies, even in the wake of the election. After the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, the White House argued in a release Trump’s tariffs and tax cuts are “bringing factories home.”

“Putting a stop to American workers, farmers, and businesses being ripped off by lopsided trade agreements has been a key foundation of President Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since he first came down the escalator,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in a statement.

“This administration has already secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments, and will continue to push for deals that deliver even more job growth, wage increases, and opportunities for hardworking Americans,” he added.

articles.title: The vanity economy is taking over America’s downtowns
articles.summary: City streets and suburban shopping malls are being reshaped by our collective obsession with appearance, health and fitness.
articles.body: QQ Nails opened its first salon in New York City twenty years ago. By 2020, QQ had grown to roughly 20 locations. It’s nearly doubled in size since the pandemic. Thirty-eight QQ salons now dot the city’s streets, with plans for dozens more. In one six block radius in Manhattan, there are four. “People are more willing to spend on self-care, self-expressiveness and these types of larger services,” CEO Tian Jiang said. Welcome to the “vanity economy.” Brick-and-mortar stores were once designed to sell you stuff: shoes, furniture and TVs. Today, they’re all about making your face, abs, hair and nails look and feel fit for the world— both the in-person and social media versions of your life. City streets and suburban shopping malls have been reconfigured in response to our collective obsession with appearance, health and performance. The transformation of retail storefronts is the physical manifestation of marketing buzzwords like “looksmaxxing,” “self-care” and “longevity.” Nail salons on every block. Med spas expanding rapidly. Pilates chains opening hundreds of clubs. High-intensity weightlifting studios, bathhouses, saunas, stretching studios, cryotherapy and IV therapy. Nationwide, more than 1 out of every 4 retail leases signed in the United States this year has been from a cosmetics, beauty service or fitness company, according to CoStar. It’s on pace to be the highest annual share on record. Physical stores to help you look good online The presence of screens everywhere helps explain the changes in the physical commercial landscape. People want to look good when they see others in real life. They also want to look good on Instagram, Hinge and TikTok. Vanity businesses serve both our in-person and digital lives simultaneously. “There is definitely ‘aesthetic creep’ that has intensified in recent years” Natalia Mehlman Petrzela, a historian of American politics and culture at The New School, said in an email. Women and gay men have long felt pressure to present themselves, but “straight men are now encompassed by the beauty-industrial complex in new ways” than the pre-looksmaxxing, social media era. Physical retail has also changed because many younger consumers prioritize smaller acts of self-improvement in an economy where traditional life milestones such as homeownership, marriage and kids, feel out of reach. Increasingly living alone and staying single, these consumers are less willing to cut back on gym memberships and manicures that help them feel healthier, stronger and more attractive. Gym and fitness studio memberships for people under 35 are growing faster than older groups, and they spend more on their monthly gym dues than older generations, according to the Health & Fitness Association. Gen Z spending at cosmetics stores was also nearly twice as strong as the overall average this year. When QQ Nails opened in 2006, manicures were seen as a “pampering moment,” Jiang said. “All you did was a polish and a clean up.” But manicures and personal care services are now associated with physical and mental well-being. Salons’ offerings and techniques have evolved, too. More expensive gel manicures and pedicures replaced regular air-dried nail polish. Customers come for extensions and custom designs they see on TikTok. More men get manicures. “It’s become more ingrained in everybody’s routines,” she said. Amazon-proof Vanity businesses have also come to dominate the streets because e-commerce has altered the utility of a storefront. As online shopping made it easier than ever to buy products from home, physical retail moved into services that couldn’t easily be duplicated online. Amazon can ship a television or pair of sneakers to your doorstep. But it can’t give you a manicure, Botox or six-pack abs. Retail leasing by service-oriented tenants outpaced goods-based tenants for the first time ever this year. It’s a shift for real estate developers and city planners who were long wary of gyms and personal-care businesses in prime retail corridors. Cities have loosened their zoning laws to make it easier for gyms, studios and spas to expand into more commercial areas in recent years. Many traditional retailers in shopping centers ended strict provisions in their leases preventing fitness tenants from locating nearby. As these lease restrictions eased, shopping centers added more boutique fitness tenants, said David Gerstenhaber, the head of leasing at Brixmor Property Group. The company owns more than 340 shopping centers around the country. Forty percent of Brixmor’s shopping centers now have a boutique fitness tenant, up from 29% in 2021. Beauty, boutique fitness, and wellness tenants like Face Foundrie and Hydration Room have grown 11% over the last five years at its properties. Lake Pointe Village, a shopping center in Sugar Land, Texas, anchored by Whole Foods, is the poster child for the shift. There are 13 vanity businesses in the center — everything from Solidcore to VIO Med Spa to European Wax Center. “It all comes down to look good, feel good,” he said.

articles.title: Shaq made a backup plan in case he lost his fortune. He says it'll pay him $1 million a month starting next year.
articles.summary: NBA icon Shaquille O'Neal spoke about his guaranteed paycheck, his early Google wager, and the "stipulations" on his children's inheritance.
articles.body:
Shaquille O'Neal says a dull insurance product will pay him $1 million a month from next spring.

The NBA icon said he "put a lot into annuities" to secure an income in case his investments failed.

O'Neal also spoke about his early Google bet and the "stipulations" on his kids' inheritance.

Shaquille O'Neal says he bought a boring financial product years ago in case he squandered his fortune, and it's poised to pay him $1 million a month starting next year.

The basketball legend known as "Shaq" told the story behind his safety net during the latest episode of the "Dinner Party" podcast. He once asked a "filthy rich guy" — a "Four Seasons, Rolls-Royce" type — how to stay rich .

The man pulled out a napkin, tore it in half, then half again, and said, "If you want to be wealthy, you play with 25, and you save 75 ."

O'Neal — who once spent $1 million in a single day when he was 20 — said he began saving aggressively following their conversation. Later, when he began investing his wealth, he wanted to lock in a future income in case those bets didn't pay off.

"So I had so much money coming in, I put a lot into annuities," the four-time NBA champion said. "That was my fail-proof just in case the investments don't work , and this and that."

An annuity is an insurance product that converts a lump sum or series of premiums into a regular stream of income payments, usually paid in retirement.

O'Neal, who's touted annuities in the past, said that after he turns 55 next spring, he'll have "a lot" coming in, "almost for the rest of my life."

Asked how much he expects to receive, he replied: "I don't like to brag, but I think at 55 I'll probably get a million dollars a month."

O'Neal made several other memorable comments on the podcast. He recalled telling his children, " We ain't rich; I'm rich ," and informing them of the "stipulations" for receiving any inheritance from him.

"Got to have a master's. Got to have a bachelor's," he said. "If you want to touch the cheese, you got to have two or three degrees."

O'Neal famously promised his mother he would return to college after turning pro to finish his degree, and went on to earn a bachelor's, a master's, and a doctorate.

He also revisited a famous moment in a hotel lobby where a stranger invited him to invest in Google , now Alphabet, before it went public.

The legendary baller said he "put in a little bit" after running the opportunity by his "money guy," and later read in the newspaper how well early investors in Google had done.

He called the Google bet a "nice big hit," but then quipped that he lost it all in his 2009 divorce , sticking his tongue out in trademark fashion.

Experiences like that may help explain O'Neal's taste for annuities, an unglamorous but reliable way to secure a retirement income.

articles.title: Wall Street's Biggest Bubble Looks Ready to Burst, and I Don't Mean AI or Quantum Computing
articles.summary: A $1.5 trillion powder keg can upend the stock market’s four-year rally.
articles.body:
Last month, Wall Street and investors celebrated the fourth anniversary of the current bull market. Both the benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and growth-fueled Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have more than doubled from their 2022 bear market lows, while the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) has rallied as much as 90%.

A confluence of factors has propelled Wall Street's major stock indexes to new heights, no two of which are larger than the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and the advent and early-stage proliferation of quantum computing. Both are trillion-dollar addressable opportunities that investors simply don't want to miss.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But following the stock market's parabolic climb, concerns are mounting about a possible AI and/or quantum computing bubble-bursting event. While history hasn't exactly been kind to next-big-thing technologies -- every game-changing technology has endured an early-innings bubble-bursting event since the mid-1990s -- there's an even more prominent bubble that looks ready to burst , based on what history tells us.

This $1.5 trillion bubble can upend the stock market's AI- and quantum computing-driven rally

While history shows that the AI and quantum computing bubbles should eventually burst, the $1.5 trillion outstanding margin debt bubble may be the spark that upends the stock market's four-year rally.

"Margin" is money an investor borrows from their broker, with interest, to wager against (short-sell) or purchase securities. When margin is used to buy stocks or exchange-traded funds (ETFs), it represents a form of leverage.

Using margin can be risky. If an investor's wager moves in the desired direction, they can quickly amplify their gains. But if a stock or ETF moves in the opposite direction, losses can be quickly magnified. This dynamic makes outstanding margin debt a somewhat crude, yet intriguing measure of investors' willingness to take risks.

According to FINRA, outstanding margin debt rocketed to an all-time high of $1.502 trillion in June. Although margin debt is expected to steadily increase over time in lockstep with the overall value of the stock market, bad things often happen when the amount investors borrow from their brokers rises dramatically over a short time frame.

articles.body:

Retirement planning is often based on several assumptions.

There's simply no way to predict how long you will live, how much inflation you will experience during your retirement and what the stock and bond markets will do over that same period.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

So you're left to plan for roughly 30 years based on some well-informed guesses.

One of those variables is market returns. Most retirees take a look at historical returns from the stock market and expect a similar return in their retirement years. Since the S&P 500 was launched in 1957, it has delivered an average annual return of 10%, according to Fidelity (1). An entire generation has probably used that 10% assumption to design all their financial plans.

Still, past performance isn't an indicator of future returns. In fact, Fidelity and Vanguard have both issued future guidance for the stock market that looks a lot less attractive than the 10% average.

Here's why U.S. retirees should pay close attention to these sobering forecasts.

Major investment firms use different methodologies to forecast stock market returns over the long term, but in general they focus on similar factors such as valuations, interest rates, inflation and earnings growth projections.

In 2026, two of the biggest firms have long-term forecasts significantly below the 10% historical average. Vanguard's 10-year outlook (2) published late October suggests U.S. stocks will deliver an average annual return between 4.8%–6.8% over the next decade. And Fidelity's forecast holds for much longer. The firm issued a 20-year forecast (3) with expectations set at 5.8% for US stocks.

Reasons for the modest forecasts include higher starting valuations, lower growth potential and frothy market conditions.

To be fair, none of the Wall Street firms have crystal balls. An educated guess based on rigorous research by an army of analysts is still just a best guess. Nevertheless, these cautious sentiments from Wall Street heavyweights should temper some of your own expectations for market returns, especially if you're in early retirement.

articles.title: How Virgin Media O2’s failed takeover gambit cost 4,000 jobs
articles.summary: When Mike Fries, the 63-year-old boss of Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) parent company Liberty Global, mounted a defence of the £2bn broadband takeover he had engine...
articles.body:
When Mike Fries, the 63-year-old boss of Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) parent company Liberty Global, mounted a defence of the £2bn broadband takeover he had engineered, his strategy was scattergun.

"Who is going to build a scale-based competitor to BT Openreach?" he said at a conference in London this year. "Who has the capital, the wherewithal, the customers? I don't think there's anybody else."

Criticism levelled at the deal by rivals was merely "sour grapes", he insisted, while simultaneously threatening to pull investment in the UK if it was blocked on competition grounds.

But his warnings fell on deaf ears. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) signalled last month that it was likely to block VMO2's takeover of Netomnia on fears it would push up prices for customers.

The apparent failure has set off fears that VMO2, owner of Britain's second-largest broadband network after BT, is headed for danger over its £22bn debt pile.

The Netomnia takeover promised a vital lifeline to help pay down this debt. With that deal on the ropes, bosses are now preparing to cut 4,000 jobs in an attempt to strip out £800m of costs.

It is a sobering shake-up for a company hoping to secure its position as the second-largest player in Britain's cut-throat broadband market. Yet some analysts warn that it might not be enough.

VMO2, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, was formed through a £31bn merger of Virgin Media and O2 in 2021.

The deal gave it the scale to compete against BT as a converged mobile and broadband operator. But it also loaded the combined company up with debt.

While Telefonica's O2 arrived debt-free, Liberty's Virgin Media contributed a £11.3bn debt pile, a legacy of the chaotic cable rollout of the 1990s.

A major debt recapitalisation, which was used to fund a £7.1bn payout to the parent companies, pushed this up above £18bn. Total debt has since climbed further to around £22.4bn.

In many ways, it was a textbook deal for Liberty Global, the Bermuda-domiciled telecoms group controlled by cable cowboy John Malone. The company had partly been attracted to Virgin Media by the lawful tax avoidance opportunities offered by its historical debts.

Liberty Global, which has its London base in plush offices just off the King's Road in Chelsea, has gained a reputation for debt-fuelled takeovers and financial engineering. Its other UK investments include Formula E, ITV and film producer Lionsgate.

To date, the merger has paid off handsomely. Liberty and Telefónica have extracted more than £12bn from VMO2 through cash payouts and dividends.

articles.title: The October jobs report just gave the Fed a new reason to hike rates: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: A blowout October jobs report revived the odds of a December Fed rate hike a day after the AI sell-off had knocked them down.
articles.body:
Thursday's AI sell-off talked traders out of a December rate hike. Friday's jobs report talked them right back in.

Chip stocks had their second-worst day since 1994 on Thursday. Polymarket's chances of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's Dec. 9 meeting sank to about 64% that day, from 81% the day before. Then employers added 165,000 jobs in October , more than double the forecast, and the probability climbed back to about 78%.

That's great news for anyone hunting for a job. It's less great for anyone hoping the Fed would ride to the rescue of a bruised and battered stock market.

The report was strong almost everywhere you looked. The unemployment rate slipped, the prior two months were revised higher, and paychecks grew faster than expected.

"With a number like this, you can put aside labor as a concern," Interactive Brokers chief strategist Steve Sosnick said on Yahoo Finance's "The 8:30."

That leaves the Fed staring at the other half of its job: inflation.

The bar for a healthy job market is lower than it used to be. Baby boomers are retiring, and immigration has slowed, so RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas figures the economy needs only about 35,000 new jobs per month to remain stable. He told Yahoo Finance's "Market Hang" he expects "job growth at more than three times what's necessary to stabilize the labor market."

Surprisingly, a cooler stock market might be part of the cure.

Wealthy households have done a lot of the spending lately, fueled by their stock gains, a pattern economists call the wealth effect . Take some air out of stocks, and some of that spending cools too.

"To the extent that higher rates also take a little steam off of equity prices, that can cool inflation by the most affluent households," KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk said on "The 8:30."

Politico's Victoria Guida floated a gentler path on Yahoo Finance's "Market Hang." She recommends slowing the AI build-out through regulation, "rather than having the Fed take a huge sledgehammer and have to raise rates a lot in order to cool some of this down."

The one corner of the job market that's shrinking

Not everyone joined the hiring spree. Tech and media jobs, which the government counts as the information sector , peaked in November 2022, the month ChatGPT launched. They've fallen about 12% since.

Healthcare and social assistance did most of the heavy lifting instead, supplying about 6 of every 10 jobs added over the past year.

Brusuelas said AI isn't moving the needle for the economy as a whole yet, even if tech and banking are seeing "a little bit less labor growth."

articles.title: Wall Street Races for Megadeals as Countdown Begins on Trump Era
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s return to the White House changed the political calculus around mergers and acquisitions, reviving companies’ desire for dream deals...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's return to the White House changed the political calculus around mergers and acquisitions, reviving companies' desire for dream deals that had become difficult to pull off. Now, corporate America is on the clock.

The rout by the Democrats in the midterms is creating a sudden sense of urgency in boardrooms, with executives wondering if they might have one last chance to pull off a transformational transaction while M&A-friendly regulators remain in place under Trump.

Conversations with top advisers suggest the result is already prompting companies to ask whether they should move fast to bring big strategic moves forward. There's a realization that a resurgent Democratic Party could work to frustrate the kind of blockbuster dealmaking that's built up steam during Trump 2.0. and powered record revenue on Wall Street.

Kevin Foley, co-head of investment banking at JPMorgan Chase & Co., one of the world's top advisory firms, said companies should be ready to transact through another complicated operating environment.

"The biggest risk may be assuming that, sooner or later, things go back to normal," New York-based Foley said. "Standing still is always an option, but when industries are changing this fast, it's the wrong one."

Fernando Rivas, a senior Wells Fargo & Co. banker, put it more starkly at an industry conference in Boston on Thursday when he said a "now or never" mentality will return to drive M&A in the near term.

Trump's two terms have accounted for an outsized share of the biggest deals. More than half of all announced transactions worth at least $50 billion and involving a US company over the past two decades have come while he was president, according to analysis of Bloomberg-compiled data.

This year alone has seen landmark combinations in mission-critical sectors like power and technology, such as this month's record-breaking $100 billion-plus takeover of laser maker Lumentum Holdings Inc. by Marvell Technology Inc. Elsewhere, the Department of Justice cleared Paramount Skydance Corp.'s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc. without antitrust remedies.

There's a particular urgency to get going with these more complex transactions. Megadeals can take months to negotiate and even longer to clear regulatory reviews around the world. Companies that wait until a 2028 presidential campaign is in full swing to move ahead with such deals risk seeing them become political footballs at the stump.

articles.summary: The good news/bad news in the aftermath of the midterm blue wave.
articles.body:
I come to you today as a humble servant of the business and investing world with both good and bad news.

First, the sprinkles of good news, because I think we can agree we need something uplifting after watching the market get torched, blown up, and shredded to pieces in the aftermath of the blue wave .

Nothing changes in D.C. overnight, if at all. Companies' fundamentals are what will drive their stock prices in the long term. I don't think the fundamentals of companies have been destroyed this week, at least not to the extent that would warrant some of the sell-offs we witnessed.

A Hut 8 ( HUT ) data center build-out isn't getting a work order stoppage today that will derail the fourth quarter numbers. Dems aren't carting off AI data center C-suites to jail and sending their companies into bankruptcy.

Texas governor-elect Hinojosa isn't sending construction crews to data centers under an order to tear them all down and turn the land into parks. Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) — based in Texas — is still operational this weekend, from what I can tell. Musk is still on pace to churn out Tesla ( TSLA ) robotaxis and robots in large numbers in 2027.

AMD ( AMD ) didn't offer a huge 2027 outlook this week on its earnings call because it fears a blue wave stopping its CPU momentum in its tracks.

In fact, AMD CEO Lisa Su told me the demand she is seeing is off the charts !

Hilton ( HLT ) CEO Chris Nassetta is so confident in his business trends that he told me this week he felt compelled to share directional guidance for 2027 with investors. Nassetta normally doesn't share these types of year-ahead specifics.

"Here's the reality. Our political system has been built pretty well," Nassetta said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Our founders did a pretty good job of creating a resilient system. We always figure it out. We'll figure it out this time. The reality is, in the next two or three years, I don't see any real dramatic impact as a result of the last couple days."

Nassetta is going on year 20 as CEO of Hilton, an almost unheard-of run in the C-suite. I don't think you get to log 20 years as Hilton CEO if you are wrong on a lot of stuff — and I think Chris makes a valid point on the political winds that are always blowing.

Now the bad news — and it's short and to the point.

We can no longer believe earnings estimates for 2027 and 2028. While in one breath I'm telling you corporate fundamentals haven't been destroyed this week, in the other breath I acknowledge they have taken a minor hit.

Data center projects won't come to a screeching halt in the US. It will just take a higher bar to get them built. And it will be costlier to get the deals done.

articles.title: Why Beneficiary Forms Decide Who Inherits Retirement and Life Insurance Accounts
articles.summary: Most Americans believe their will distributes their estate, but that’s not the case with retirement accounts, life insurance, and more.
articles.body:
Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, life insurance and payable-on-death accounts override wills in most cases.

Failing to update beneficiary forms after major life events can lead to unintended outcomes.

Wills govern assets without beneficiary designations, such as real estate, personal property, and vehicles.

The dramatic reading of the will in a wood-paneled office has long been a staple of television dramas. The question of who's in—or not in—the will is a go-to for murder whodunnits, and there's good reason the premise lands: Many Americans believe the will has the final say over their legacy.

The truth, though, is that for much of what typical Americans leave behind—retirement accounts, life insurance, and bank accounts with a payable-on-death designation—the will means little. What matters is the beneficiary form you filled out and, often, forgot about when you opened those accounts. That's what dictates who gets what when you die.

More than $49.1 trillion was held in U.S. retirement accounts—like and ,—and in as of 2025, according to the Investment Company Institute. Not a dollar of it will ever pass through a will.

Instead, the funds will be distributed according to the beneficiary designations listed on a form on file with your financial institution. The same rule applies to policies and any bank or brokerage account with a or designation.

About three in four Americans don't have a will, according to a Caring.com survey.

"Beneficiary forms are extremely powerful and trump whatever it might say in the will in most or all circumstances," said Ari Weisbard, a certified financial planner and attorney at Values Added.

There's a real benefit to this: your loved ones don't have to wait for a probate court to rule to get money for your funeral or their own needs. Except in rare instances, the beneficiary form is the final word. For example, if your will names your spouse as the beneficiary of your IRA but the account designates your children, the money will go to your kids, even if your updated your will recently.

Still, if you've forgotten about those beneficiary forms, you're not alone.

"Some people leave retirement accounts in place with old beneficiaries when they leave their job," Weisbard said. "If they listed their friend or sibling as the beneficiary, that might still govern even if they got married or had kids later."

articles.title: Oracle Just Walked Away From a $7 Billion Tencent Deal. Here’s What It Means for ORCL Stock.
articles.summary: Oracle's abandoned $7 billion Tencent chip deal adds uncertainty, but accelerating revenue and a massive AI backlog could offer investors a compelling opport...
articles.body:
Wall Street is having a tough sell-off moment. And not a good one. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped by almost 5.5% Thursday after a significant sell-off that coincided with worries over U.S. midterm election outcomes. It officially fell into correction mode, reversed its post-election rally, and erased a record $2.5 trillion in market value.

Along with that, Oracle (ORCL) has been absolutely hammered this year. Shares of ORCL are down 40% year-to-date (YTD). That is a brutal stretch for a company that was supposed to be one of the biggest winners of the AI boom.

But here is where things get interesting. Oracle just walked away from a $7 billion chip leasing deal with Tencent (TCEHY). And that might actually be a blessing in disguise.

Let's talk about the pain first. ORCL hit a 52-week low of $111.6 on Thursday.

The reasons are many. Broader market sell-off; immense capital expenditure costs are being seen in terms of AI data centers. People are too ticked off about their debt. The Tencent cancellation now brings additional uncertainty to the nervous market.

But there's this in the headlines: Oracle isn't resting on its laurels, and that's not an understatement. The company is taking a very controversial step that may change the course of its future.

Earlier this year, Oracle inked a five-year agreement with Tencent involving the deployment of approximately 100,000 chips of state-of-the-art AI at data centers in the Southeast Asian region. The estimated value was $7 billion. Tencent decided to pay about 30% in advance.

Then, Washington got involved. US authorities were concerned. Oracle listened. The company walked-off.

So does this negatively impact Oracle? Honestly, not much. The deal was not on the official list of Oracle's products. The rest of Oracle's engagements for performance are a whopping $664 billion. A gap of $7 billion seems a trifle, if nothing more. When Tencent loses money, it's more than the "fundamentals."

Oracle reported fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on September 10. And the numbers were spectacular. Revenue topped $19.3 billion, a record high. This is an increase of 30% from the previous year. Net income grew to $4.7 billion, above the level at the same time last year by 60%. Adjusted earnings per share stood at $1.92, up 30%. It also had record operating cash flow of $23 billion. Oracle continued to invest in infrastructure used for AI, and that caused free cash flow to be negative $5 billion. Cash and cash equivalents as of the end of FY 2026 were approximately $31.3 billion.

articles.title: Wall Street hiring helps lift finance jobs in October
articles.summary: Firms in financial activities-related businesses added 7,000 jobs last month, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Friday. The additions mar...
articles.body:
Hiring across the financial sector showed signs of life in October, with Wall Street-related firms adding workers, while commercial lending and insurers continued to shed jobs.

Firms in financial activities-related businesses added 7,000 jobs last month, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Friday. The additions mark the first net hiring gain in that corner of the labor market since June, leaving the financial services sector with about 99,000 fewer jobs than it had a year ago.

Along with real estate roles, Wall Street-related positions helped lift October hiring by 2,900 jobs.

Employment in securities, commodity contracts, funds, trusts, investments, and related activities — a broad category encompassing much of Wall Street and the asset management industry — rose by 2,900 in October and is up roughly 29,000 from a year ago.

"Across the board, things are really active," Brianne Sterling, who leads investment banking recruiting in New York for Selby Jennings, said in a Thursday interview.

Sterling told Yahoo Finance the firm has seen strong hiring across financial services, especially in investment banking.

"This has been, I think, one of our best years ever" for recruiting, Sterling added, likening 2026 to the post-COVID hiring boom of 2022.

Senior investment bankers are switching jobs at an unusually active pace. Sterling said Selby Jennings typically tracks roughly 20 to 30 managing director-level investment banking moves per month, but counted nearly 50 in September.

Not every business within the financial services sector rose last month. Commercial banking shed another 1,200 jobs in October and now employs about 26,000 fewer people than a year ago, while insurance employment fell by 5,500 last month and is down nearly 90,000 from October 2025.

Collectively, the six largest US banks reported a year-over-year decline in headcount in the third quarter, with those figures also suggesting selective hiring as opposed to a broad effort to shrink labor forces.

JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Goldman Sachs ( GS ), and Morgan Stanley ( MS ) each increased headcount during the third quarter, while Bank of America (BAC), Citigroup ( C ), and Wells Fargo ( WFC ) reduced some positions.

The uneven hiring wave comes as banks are still aggressively looking to automate tasks or rely on fewer workers with newer artificial intelligence tools at their disposal, Sterling added.

The industry is also navigating a tricky environment amid rising borrowing costs. Higher Treasury yields have increased unrealized losses on their bond portfolios and raised concerns about borrowing activity. The KBW Nasdaq Bank Index ( ^BKX ) was about 12% below its August high as of Friday afternoon, though it remains up more than 4% year to date.

articles.title: Fiat's tiny Topolino is a $15K microcar that's tapping into America's golf-cart boom
articles.summary: There's a new tiny car in town, and America might be into it
articles.body:
There's a new tiny car in town, and America just might be into it.

Fiat ( STLA ) brought the Topolino to the US this year, a golf cart-like electric car with a heritage design. Topolino, or "little mouse" in Italian, harkens back to the original Topolino, which Fiat built from 1936 to 1955. That small car, known for its Mickey Mouse-style headlamps, eventually grew into the iconic Fiat 500.

Fiat initially planned to sell the new Topolino in Europe for people living in small towns (think beach towns or hilly villages) or even for large resorts. And while that has been the case, the company decided to run a small test by offering 300 Topolinos to its dealers in the US.

"The original shipment was 300 units - the majority of those have already been sold," said Andrew Waterhouse, head of Fiat North America, to Yahoo Finance. "We're taking it step by step, because like I said, it's kind of an experiment."

Waterhouse points to a booming market for what the industry calls micromobility, which he says Fiat's data shows will grow 28% over the next five years. Right now that demand shows up mostly as street-legal golf carts.

"Those people aren't using golf carts … to play golf," he said. They're using them "to drive around, to go to lunch, to drive to the pool, drive to the beach."

For Fiat, who still sells the 500e in the US, it's a natural. "We've always been known for small cars," Waterhouse said. "If there's one brand, I think I would say that could go even smaller, it's us."

The Topolino starts at around $15,000 with destination, and Fiat offers free home delivery within 50 miles of the selling dealer.

About 60% of US buyers have chosen the open-air Dolce Vita edition, which swaps doors for ropes. In Europe, the version with doors is more popular. "If you're living in a city … you want to be able to lock your stuff in your car," Waterhouse said. In the US, he said, the Dolce Vita suits "a beach town, gated community resort type experience where you want the open air."

Styling-wise, the Topolino is a winner - it just exudes that Italian style that Fiats are known for - at least historically. The car initially came in Verde Vita (green life) Mint, but for 2027 will be offered in Corallo Orange (sun-kissed coral) and Luna Greige (gray moon).

Interior-wise, the car is very basic, lots of plastic, but some fun elements like the top dashboard glovebox with leather straps, and special Bluetooth speakers that come in matching colors and say "Ciao!" the minute they are turned on.

articles.title: 2 big AI narratives wrestle with each other: What to watch this week
articles.summary: The data center-powered sell-off leaves a lot of questions to be answered this week, and investors will get a new batch of inflation data to help parse the s...
articles.body:
Even before the sell-off last week, we've all had the feeling of white-knuckling through the fourth quarter.

Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO prospectus. Big Tech earnings. Bond yields through the roof. An unexpectedly tall blue wave that lifted the stock market up — and threw it back down.

With volatility ( ^VIX ) running hot, investors are balancing on a knife's edge between a flywheel of angst — or a bounce.

As Goldman Sachs' panic gauge suggested, the extremeness may signal more of Friday's bounce to come.

It's a new week, and we'll have plenty of scheduled plot points to guide us.

Of particular note, we're looking forward to CoreWeave ( CRWV ) quarterly results on Tuesday and Nebius Group ( NBIS ) and Cerebras Systems ( CBRS ) on Thursday, a few companies caught up in the data center destruction post-election.

What they have to say about their plans and outlook, the debt markets they've been tapping, and the health of their business will be at the top of mind.

Good timing to have that a mere week after midterms.

On the economic calendar, we're in inflation mode once again, especially after that hot jobs report.

We'll kick off the week with the New York Fed's consumer inflation expectations before getting some actual data on Tuesday — and wholesale inflation figures on Friday to close the week.

2 big AI narratives keep wrestling with each other for control of the market

What's more important: the chip and AI infrastructure trade or the companies that actually provide AI?

As we wrote in the Morning Brief on Friday, "A data center slowdown is bad for the stock market's AI engine," and "A data center slowdown is good for Big Tech's profit machine."

Can Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) deliver AI at least some productivity and tools to clients with the compute they have — and make a lot of money doing so, flipping the switch from growth and scale to monetization?

Maybe! Those companies are healthily in the green since the election, doing just fine amid the broader sell-off. And while Tesla ( TSLA ) has sold off, SpaceX ( SPCX ) is mostly doing fine.

As DataTrek's Nicholas Colas wrote on Thursday, you need to look at the entire week, not just the bloody Thursday, to see the bigger picture (small as that is). And it's pretty clear that this may be reflected in the broad indexes, but it's mostly about chips.

"As for what the market is 'saying' over the last 2 days, we believe the moves are AI-centric, not augurs of a looming recession," Colas wrote, also noting that Google and Co. are doing fine.

articles.title: Blackstone Real Estate Seeks Rebound From Shock Exits and Losses
articles.summary: David Levine and Giovanni Cutaia take over a division that has gone from the firm’s fastest growing to its slowest.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Steve Schwarzman was concerned. It had been a rough stretch for Blackstone's real estate division. The market was brutal, and the shooting death of Wesley LePatner at the firm's New York headquarters nearly a year earlier still weighed heavily on the group.

To try to raise morale, Schwarzman invited top leaders from Blackstone's real estate business to his Manhattan apartment for dinner in June. The billionaire founder and his handpicked heir apparent, Jon Gray, wanted to see firsthand how they were holding up.

Over the course of the meal, Schwarzman played both coach and cheerleader. He emphasized how important real estate was to Blackstone's legacy and to its future. He was confident that market conditions were finally improving. Under new leader Nadeem Meghji, the group would lay the groundwork for a $30 billion fundraise later in the year.

Lifting spirits further, staff members delivered periodic updates from the NBA finals game underway at Madison Square Garden: The New York Knicks continued to defy odds and expectations. Anything seemed possible.

But the five months since have only brought more tumult for a group that was once a crown jewel for the $1.4 trillion firm. In September, Meghji, the head of the unit, announced his plans to leave, less than 10 months after the departure of his former co-head Kathleen McCarthy. The real estate market is getting slammed yet again by higher rates, the group's profit is tracking at half its 2022 peak, and the anticipated flagship fundraise has been delayed.

Blackstone's most recent financial results revealed another disappointing quarter for the real estate group. Distributable earnings for the group fell 10% from the same quarter a year earlier, assets were down $30 billion from their peak, and its opportunistic strategies lost 3.2% in three months. Blackstone's private equity division has dethroned real estate as the most profitable business in the firm.

The firm tapped David Levine and Giovanni Cutaia to shore up the unit, all under the watchful eye of Gray, who built the business and remains actively involved. The duo has to persuade investors that they can steady the ship, and they need to close new deals before they can raise more money.

articles.title: Cheaper Scotch squeezes local distillers
articles.summary: Cheaper Scotch after India-UK duty cuts is squeezing small Indian distillers, as imported labels undercut local whisky; bulk imports may lower prices 8–10%.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Cheaper Scotch is putting Indian whisky makers under pressure, even as lower import duties offer savings to companies that use it in their blends. For small distillers that make their own spirits, an imported label can now cost substantially less than a locally made bottle.Huli’s rice malt whisky was launched in Karnataka at Rs 2,650 for 750ml. By comparison, J&B Rare was priced at Rs 1,375 at Bengaluru retailer Tonique in October, according to TOI’s earlier reporting. At these prices, J&B Rare cost Rs 1,275 less, or about half as much. Tonique said the price had fallen from Rs 2,835, attributing the reduction to local bottling.“The smaller players will not be able to survive,” said Huli Spirits founder Aruna Urs. Her Mysuru distillery makes spirits from locally sourced paddy and jaggery and does not import Scotch.Arun Kumar Parasa of Unistil Alcoblends said falling Scotch prices had adversely affected the Indian single malt industry. Lower duties on bulk Scotch imported by some small and medium distilleries would benefit them “very marginally”, he said.The distinction is between making spirits locally and buying imported whisky for bottling or blending. Bulk Scotch arrives in large containers and can be bottled here or used as an ingredient in Indian whisky. A lower import bill can help these manufacturers, while cheaper finished bottles intensify competition for other producers.Jason Holway, senior consultant at drinks research firm IWSR, expects the price gap to narrow further. “Depending on the state, cheaper blended Scotches are expected to become more attractively priced than they used to be and may not be much more expensive than domestic premium brands using Scotch as an ingredient.”India’s trade agreement with Britain cut Scotch import duties from 150% to 75%. Customs officials subsequently questioned whether certain bulk shipments qualified for the lower duty. On Nov 2, commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal assured manufacturers that the duty benefits would be protected, with commerce and revenue officials to work on resolving the classification dispute.An industry executive, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Indian buyers were also negotiating better purchase prices from Scotland. The executive estimated that the duty reduction could lower retail prices by roughly 8-10%, depending on state taxes and companies’ pricing decisions. Distribution difficulties and advertising restrictions remained longstanding hurdles for small manufacturers, the executive added.IWSR’s figures also show the limits of India’s shift towards expensive whisky. Its premium-and-above category, defined as Rs 2,899.01 or more per 750ml bottle, accounted for less than 1% of whisky consumed by volume in 2025, Holway said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over foreign intelligence concerns
articles.summary: Nvidia announced Sunday that it is launching an independent investigation into its chief executive and founder Jensen Huang over concerns that he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
articles.body: Nvidia announced Sunday it is launching an independent investigation into its chief executive and founder, Jensen Huang, over concerns he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The statement, published on the company’s website, comes after US officials have expressed concern over Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company. (The two are not related). Separately, Huang admitted having an extramarital affair in a note to staff, though he did not name the woman. The Financial Times previously reported that US officials believed the two were in a romantic relationship. Several outlets have reported that American officials suspect Alice Huang has fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips to the country. Nvidia is the world’s leading chipmaker amid the AI boom and has a market capitalization of about $4.5 trillion. CNN has asked the State Department for comment. The company previously said in a statement that Jensen Huang’s meetings were “not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.” Nvidia said a committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee its investigation. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” “Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN. Jensen Huang, 63, said that he was “unfaithful” and hurt his wife and children in the note to Nvidia staff. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Jensen Huang said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Nvidia's board launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly admitted to employees that he had an affair, following allegations of a romantic relationship with a woman suspected of be...
articles.body:
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board is launching an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government.

In a email to employees Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair.

"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote.

"To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," the CEO added.

In a statement Sunday, the board said it "a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation" into the matter.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said statement.

The revelations come after reports of ties between Huang and a woman believed to be passing information to the Chinese government.

Last month, the New York Times reported the US intelligence service believed a Chinese national named Alice Huang, a former leader at Megaspeed, an Nvidia chip customer, and someone with a well-documented relationship with Huang himself, may have acted as an intelligence asset , sharing information with the ruling party in Beijing.

Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives wrote in a note to investors on Sunday that the investigation is a "black eye" for Huang and will likely spark multiple congressional investigations.

"The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?….The investigation will be key and we would expect Jensen to continue in his role as CEO with no interruption in the near-term," Ives wrote.

"There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally. This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China which remains a key battleground issue in DC," he added.

The US government banned the sale of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, though the company has lobbied to continue offering the hardware saying it is better if the world uses processors from a US business.
